groups.instruction: Complete the sentences below. Write ONE WORD for each answer.

parts.context: A lecturer summarises research on bilingual education.

transcript.text: Good morning. Around half of the world's population speaks more than one language, and in many countries schools teach in two languages. Today I'll look at what research says about the effects of bilingual education on children.
transcript.speaker: DR MENDEZ

transcript.text: I should make clear what I mean by bilingual education. I do not mean one hour of foreign language lessons per week. I mean programmes in which children use two languages for learning subjects such as science or history over a long period of time.
transcript.speaker: DR MENDEZ

transcript.text: Early research claimed that bilingualism confused children and held back their development. Those claims were made in the nineteen twenties. We now know that these studies were flawed, partly because the children tested came from poor families and had received little schooling.
transcript.speaker: DR MENDEZ

transcript.text: Later, a Canadian study changed this view. It showed that bilingual children performed better in tests of attention and problem solving, and other researchers soon confirmed the result.
transcript.speaker: DR MENDEZ

transcript.text: This is an important lesson about how research develops. A result that seems convincing in one decade can look very weak a few years later, when scientists have better methods and more careful samples, and that is why we should always look for repeated evidence.
transcript.speaker: DR MENDEZ

transcript.text: One explanation is that bilinguals constantly switch between languages, which trains the brain's executive function, the system that controls attention and decision making.
transcript.speaker: DR MENDEZ

transcript.text: Another benefit appears later in life. Some studies suggest that bilingual people develop symptoms of dementia about four years later than those who speak one language.
transcript.speaker: DR MENDEZ

transcript.text: Of course, one should be careful. Researchers still debate how large the effect is, and some recent studies have found smaller differences than the early ones. It is probably more accurate to say that bilingualism does no harm and may bring some advantages.
transcript.speaker: DR MENDEZ

transcript.text: Of course, not all programmes are equally successful. The most effective model is called immersion, in which children spend at least half of the school day learning subjects in the second language.
transcript.speaker: DR MENDEZ

transcript.text: Other models include the transitional approach, where children study in their home language for the first years and then move to the second language, and the dual-language approach, where half the class speaks each language and they learn from each other.
transcript.speaker: DR MENDEZ

transcript.text: Successful programmes share several features. First, teachers must be fully fluent in both languages, because children copy their pronunciation and grammar.
transcript.speaker: DR MENDEZ

transcript.text: Second, parents need support. Some parents worry that using their home language will hurt progress in the school language, but research shows the opposite, so schools should hold regular meetings to explain this.
transcript.speaker: DR MENDEZ

transcript.text: Third, assessment must be fair. If a child is tested only in the second language, the results may show their language level rather than their knowledge of the subject.
transcript.speaker: DR MENDEZ

transcript.text: Fourth, the materials matter. Good programmes provide books in both languages so children can compare words and ideas.
transcript.speaker: DR MENDEZ

transcript.text: Finally, patience is essential. It usually takes five to seven years for a child to reach the same level in the second language as native speakers, so results in the first year can be disappointing.
transcript.speaker: DR MENDEZ

transcript.text: There is one more point I would like to stress. Motivation matters enormously, so programmes that make the second language feel useful and enjoyable, with songs, games and real communication, tend to produce better results than those that rely on drills.
transcript.speaker: DR MENDEZ

transcript.text: Thank you. In the seminar we'll look at a case study from Wales.
transcript.speaker: DR MENDEZ
